lesson_title: The Grip That Lets You Walk
hook_text: Without friction you could not take a single step. Here is the force that grips, pulls and pushes.
clip_script: Try walking on ice in socks and you discover friction by missing it. Friction is the grip between two surfaces, and it always fights sliding. Under a microscope every surface is bumpy, and the bumps catch. Rough surfaces and heavy loads mean more friction; oil, wheels and smooth surfaces mean less. Friction lets you walk, lets taxis brake and lets you hold a pen. That is why tyres have treads. But it also wears out tyres and wastes energy as heat, which is why engines need oil. Now two more contact forces. Tension is the pull inside a stretched rope or cable, like the steel cables holding up the Nelson Mandela Bridge. Ropes can only pull. Compression is the squash inside a pillar or a table leg. Concrete loves compression but hates tension, so builders hide steel bars inside it.
visual_style: Socks sliding on tiles; a microscope zoom on rough surfaces; tyre treads in rain; the Nelson Mandela Bridge cables at sunset; a pillar being squeezed with arrows.
mood: Playful start, then confident and engineering-focused.
pacing: Funny opening slip, brisk explanation, a sweeping bridge shot and a crisp finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and spot tension and compression in your school buildings.
